extracted.intended_audience: sketch comedy writers, SNL hopefuls, late-night writers and performers interested in Mike O'Brien's writing approach
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and pitching sketch comedy in the vein of Mike O'Brien / SNL: using frames, real interactions, and committed worlds to generate humor, plus pitch-night practice. Focuses on premise, world-building, framing, and pitch performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found Joke (frame-based comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mike O'Brien's signature is finding the comedic moment in a real interaction (7 Minutes in Heaven). The interview structure CREATES the joke; the celebrity is the foil. This is the unscripted comedy of FRAMING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an authentic interaction or constraint as the source of comedy rather than inventing purely gag lines. Design a structure (the frame) that brings out an opponent/foil reaction — the humor comes from how a real person navigates that frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame as the primary comedic device
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame imposes RULES (you must answer in the closet, with no preparation). The audience laughs at the celebrity navigating the imposed rules. The frame is the joke; the dialogue is the execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When devising a sketch, explicitly define the rules and constraints that participants must follow; ensure those rules create tension/awkwardness or a repeated comic situation. Treat dialogue as the mechanism to reveal how the frame produces comedy. Anti-pattern: weak or ill-defined frames that don't shape behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the FRAME of the piece doing comedic work?
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien-Inflected Working Rubric item: 'Is the FRAME of the piece doing comedic work?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the conceit or structural constraint itself generates laughs (through rule-based conflict, awkwardness, or forced behavior), not only whether the lines are funny. If removing the frame leaves only disconnected jokes, the frame may not be doing enough work.

rubrics_metrics.name: World played straight despite its absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien's SNL sketches often had a single bizarre premise played fully straight. The straightness is the joke; the world's commitment to the absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to the internal logic of the sketch — act as if the absurd premise is normal. Strong examples: 'Diner Lobster' and 'Chris Pine: Hilarious Disaster.' Anti-pattern: winking at the audience or undercutting the premise with meta-jokes that dissolve the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the premise generate, or just repeat?
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien-Inflected Working Rubric item: 'Does the premise generate, or just repeat?' Also stated: 'A sketch that's ONE joke played four times is a bad sketch. A sketch that's ONE WORLD with multiple jokes within it is a good sketch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the central premise spawns a variety of behaviors, escalations, and comedic beats (one world → multiple jokes) versus relying on the same single gag repeated. Anti-patterns: sketches that rely on repetition of the same punchline without variation or escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching as performance — pitch with energy
rubrics_metrics.description: On Pitching at SNL: Monday is pitch night: each writer pitches 3–5 sketches to the host. The host picks favorites; the writer drafts by Wednesday. 'Pitch as performance: how you pitch determines whether it gets written.' O'Brien rubic: 'Did you pitch with energy?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pitches as a live performance: deliver your premise clearly, quickly, and with enthusiasm. Prepare 3–5 solid concepts for pitch night; prioritize the strongest. Timing: pitch Monday, draft quickly if chosen (by Wednesday). Anti-pattern: flat, vague, or overly long pitches that fail to sell the frame/world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find comedy in real-world constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien-Inflected Working Rubric item: 'Have you found the comedy in real-world constraints?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for humor that arises from natural limits or social rules (awkward protocols, etiquette, location-specific constraints). Use those constraints to force characters into funny decisions or reactions. This ties back to the 'found joke' approach: the environment supplies the comedic lever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to the bit
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien-Inflected Working Rubric item: 'Are you committing to the bit completely?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure performers and writing fully embrace the conceit without hedging. Commitment means acting, writing, and staging as if the premise is real — which increases laugh payoff. Anti-pattern: half-hearted commitment, frequent escapes into explanation or self-awareness that reduce comedic tension.
